ColumnDefinitions.title: Sharpe Ratio
ColumnDefinitions.columnDesc: Sharpe ratio is a risk-adjusted measure of performance developed by William Sharpe, also know as the reward-to-volatility ratio.  It is similar to the Information Ratio except that it uses returns in excess of the risk free rate rather than total returns.  The Sharpe ratio then, becomes the slope of the Capital Allocation Line, which is the line tangent to the efficient frontier of risky asset and defines the combination of the tangency risk portfolio and the risk-free asset.  It is calculated as the average sub-period excess return divided by the standard deviation of subperiod excess returns over a given period. Sub-period excess return is the difference between the investment return and the risk-free return for a sub-period. A higher Sharpe ratio can suggest constitency in achieving positive active returns.

ColumnDefinitions.title: Alpha t-score (Jensen)
ColumnDefinitions.columnDesc: The Jensen Regression applies a least-squares linear regression calculation to the sub-period portfolio and benchmark returns in excess of the risk free rate for a statistic period to arrive at a slope that represents the Beta of the portfolio relative to the benchmark and a verticle intercept that represents the Alpha: The portion of the active return that is not explained by the portfolio's beta relative to the benchmark.  The respective t-scores are calculated using the standard 'Student's t-distribution' and reflects the significance or reliability of the regression to describe the active return, with larger t-scores representing a stronger relationship.  As a general rule, a t-stat value greater than or equal to 2 or less than or equal to -2 indicates that the tested metric is significant at 95% confidence.

ColumnDefinitions.title: Sector Allocation
ColumnDefinitions.columnDesc:
Sector allocation return can be computed in two ways:

1) Absolute method - outperformance is the result of overweighting sectors with positive performance (or underweighting sector's with negative performance)

	Absolute Sector Allocation Return = (Wp - Wb) * (ERb)
		Wp = portfolio weight for a given sector
		Wb = benchmark weight for a given sector
		ERb = benchmark excess return for a given sector

2) Relative method - outperformance is the result of overweighting sectors with positive performance relative to the benchmark's total return (or underweighting sectors with negative performance relative to the benchmark's total return)

	Relative Sector Allocation Return = (Wp - Wb) * (ERb - ERB)
		Wp = portfolio weight for a given sector
		Wb = benchmark weight for a given sector
		ERb = benchmark excess return for a given sector
		ERB = overall benchmark excess return

	Relative Subsector Allocation Return = (Wp - Wb) * (ERb - ERB)
		Wp = portfolio weight for a given sector
		Wb = benchmark weight for a given sector
		ERb = benchmark excess return for a given subsector
		ERB = parent sector benchmark excess return

Spread duration-based allocation and selection are meaningful measures of exposure for portfolio that use of instruments that create spread exposure without significant market value (e.g. credit derivatives).  

Using spread duration contribution, sector allocation is calculated as follows:

Sector Allocation = Active Spread Duration Contribution * Benchmark Excess Return per Year of Spread Duration

To calculate the sub-sector allocation:

Subsector Allocation = [ Wport -  (Wbench * (Wport parent  / Wbench parent)) ] * (Excess - Excessparent)

	Wport = portfolio sub-sector spread duration contribution
	Wbench = benchmark sub-sector spread duration contribution
	Wport parent = portfolio sector spread duration contribution
	Wbench parent = benchmark sector spread duration contribution
	Excess = benchmark sub-sector excess return per spread duration year
	Excessparent = benchmark sector excess return per spread duration year

ColumnDefinitions.title: OAS Change Contribution

ColumnDefinitions.title: Security Selection

Security selection seeks to answer the question of whether the basket of securities purchased by the PM for a given sector performed better or worse than the securities held in the benchmark for that same sector.  There are two ways a PM can earn positive security selection return:
  
1) The portfolio can overweight a security relative to the benchmark that has positive performance (and underweight a security that has negative performance).
  
2) The portfolio can invest in out-of-benchmark securities that have positive performance and belong to the same sector. 

Security Selection Return = Wp * (ERp - ERb)
	Wp = portfolio weight for a given sector
	ERp = portfolio excess return for a given sector
	ERb = benchmark excess return for a given sector

Using spread duration contribution, security selection is calculated as follows:

Security Selection = Portfolio Spread Duration Contribution * Active Excess Return per Year of Spread Duration

Since short-term inflation expectations can be different than long-term ones, this attribution factor uses the portfolio's inflation KRD's to capture price sensitivity to various maturities along the inflation curve.

The respective t-scores are calculated using the standard 'Student's t-distribution' and reflects the significance or reliability of the regression to describe the active return, with larger t-scores representing a stronger relationship.  As a general rule, a t-stat value greater than or equal to 2 or less than or equal to -2 indicates that the tested metric is significant at 95% confidence.

ColumnDefinitions.title: Active Curve Contribution

First, the model uses the security's key-rate durations and the changes in the curve at each respective point to calculate the total interest rate return.

The P&L due to the change in the shape of the yield curve is calculated as the residual of the total interest rate change minus the P&L due to the parallel shift.

Curve Return = KRD Return - Duration Return

ColumnDefinitions.title: Benchmark Rolldown Contribution
ColumnDefinitions.columnDesc:
The daily-linked benchmark rolldown return multiplied by the security weight.

Rolldown return incorporates two effects:

1. Carry Effect - The basis earned between the overnight risk-free rate and the risk-free rate for maturities that are longer than the overnight rate.

2. The effect of the passage of time on the discount factors and discounting terms for each of the bond's cash flows.  Assuming no optionality, there are two common factors associated with the passage of time that affect the price of a security:

	-Amortization/Accretion towards par - this is reflected in the price change coming from the increase/decrease in the term over which each of the bond's cash flows is discounted

	-The shape of the yield curve - in upward-sloping yield curve environments, for example, the bond will earn positive return as each of the security's cash flows is discounted by a smaller factor.  

Active rolldown return is essentially a function of the portfolio's cash flow distribution along the yield curve relative to its benchmark.  A portfolio that is short duration relative to its benchmark will generally have negative active rolldown return, as long as the yield curve is upward sloping.

Active OAS Change Contribution
ColumnDefinitions.columnDesc:
The difference between the daily-linked portfolio OAS carry return and the daily-linked benchmark OAS carry return.

OAS Change Return is the return that can be attributed to changes in credit spreads.  For instance, if the fund invests in corporate bonds and some of those corporate issuers are downgraded by the ratings agencies, then the portfolio will see its OAS widen over the course of the performance period assuming everything remains constant.  The OAS widening occurred because investors are demanding a higher return since those corporate issuers are now perceived to be more risky.  As a result, the price of the bonds already issued by those same corporations declined since it is less certain now that lenders will receive all of their principal and interest payments on time.  We evaluate the impact of the change in a security's OAS by using the security's sensitivity to changes in spreads, which is captured in the spread duration analytic:

OAS Change Return = Spread Duration * -(Change in OAS)

ColumnDefinitions.title: Treynor Ratio

It is calculated as the average portfolio return in excess of the risk free rate divided by the beta from the Jensen regresssion.  The Treynor ratio represents the slope of the Securities Market Line, which defines the expected relationship between risk (beta) and return.  A higher Treynor ratio implies superior portfolio performance.

If inflation expectations are expected to increase over the performance period, the PM would buy more inflation-linked securities than the benchmark.   Since short-term inflation expectations can be different than long-term ones, this attribution factor uses the portfolio's inflation KRD's to capture price sensitivity to various maturities along the inflation curve.

ColumnDefinitions.title: Rolldown P&L
ColumnDefinitions.columnDesc:
Rolldown P&L incorporates two effects:

1. Carry Effect - The basis earned between the overnight risk-free rate and the risk-free rate for maturities that are longer than the overnight rate.

2. The effect of the passage of time on the discount factors and discounting terms for each of the bond's cash flows.  Assuming no optionality, there are two common factors associated with the passage of time that affect the price of a security:

	-Amortization/Accretion towards par - this is reflected in the price change coming from the increase/decrease in the term over which each of the bond's cash flows is discounted

	-The shape of the yield curve - in upward-sloping yield curve environments, for example, the bond will earn positive return as each of the security's cash flows is discounted by a smaller factor.  

Active rolldown return is essentially a function of the portfolio's cash flow distribution along the yield curve relative to its benchmark.  A portfolio that is short duration relative to its benchmark will generally have negative active rolldown return, as long as the yield curve is upward sloping.

Rolldown return incorporates two effects:

1. Carry Effect - The basis earned between the overnight risk-free rate and the risk-free rate for maturities that are longer than the overnight rate.

2. The effect of the passage of time on the discount factors and discounting terms for each of the bond's cash flows.  Assuming no optionality, there are two common factors associated with the passage of time that affect the price of a security:

	-Amortization/Accretion towards par - this is reflected in the price change coming from the increase/decrease in the term over which each of the bond's cash flows is discounted

	-The shape of the yield curve - in upward-sloping yield curve environments, for example, the bond will earn positive return as each of the security's cash flows is discounted by a smaller factor.  

Active rolldown return is essentially a function of the portfolio's cash flow distribution along the yield curve relative to its benchmark.  A portfolio that is short duration relative to its benchmark will generally have negative active rolldown return, as long as the yield curve is upward sloping.

ColumnDefinitions.title: Beta (Simple)
ColumnDefinitions.columnDesc: The Simple Regression applies a least-squares linear regression calculation to the sub-period portfolio and benchmark returns for the Statistic Period to arrive at a slope that represents the Beta of the portfolio relative to the benchmark and a verticle intercept that represents the Alpha: The portion of the active return that is not explained by the portfolio's beta relative to the benchmark.  The respective t-scores are calculated using the standard 'Student's t-distribution' and reflects the significance or reliability of the regression to describe the active return, with larger t-scores representing a stronger relationship. ColumnDefinitions.title: Benchmark Curve Contribution
ColumnDefinitions.columnDesc:
The daily-linked benchmark curve return multiplied by the security weight.

While duration return captures the majority of the effect of the change in the yield curve, curve return represents the effect of the reshaping of the yield curve, i.e. the effect of the non-parallel changes in the yield curve.

First, the model uses the security's key-rate durations and the changes in the curve at each respective point to calculate the total interest rate return.

The P&L due to the change in the shape of the yield curve is calculated as the residual of the total interest rate change minus the P&L due to the parallel shift.

Curve Return = KRD Return - Duration Return

ColumnDefinitions.title: Correlation (R) (Jensen)
ColumnDefinitions.columnDesc: Jensen Correlation measures how the excess return over risk free rate of the portfolio and benchmark are related. It ranges from -1 (perfect negative correlation) to +1 (perfect positive correlation). Negative correlation indicates that they move in opposite directions; positive correlation indicates that they move up or down together. Correlation between -0.3 and 0.3 usually signifies a weak relationship between the Fund and the Benchmark, while correlation above 0.7 and below -0.7 signifies a strong relationship.

ColumnDefinitions.title: Recovery Rate

There are two recovery rates: calibration and pricing. The calibration rate is used to generate CDS implied default probabilities while the pricing rate is used for valuation. 
 
a) If the MIP curve is exactly matched, then the pricing rate is the same as the calibration rate given by MIP.

b) If match is not exact, then calibration and pricing rates may be different
 The calibration rate is taken as 40% (when available, JPM data is used)
 The pricing rate is estimated from historical averages at sector and tier levels (based on historical MIPS data)

ColumnDefinitions.title: Active Rolldown Contribution
ColumnDefinitions.columnDesc:
The difference between the daily-linked portfolio rolldown return and the daily-linked benchmark rolldown return.

Rolldown return incorporates two effects:

1. Carry Effect - The basis earned between the overnight risk-free rate and the risk-free rate for maturities that are longer than the overnight rate.

2. The effect of the passage of time on the discount factors and discounting terms for each of the bond's cash flows.  Assuming no optionality, there are two common factors associated with the passage of time that affect the price of a security:

	-Amortization/Accretion towards par - this is reflected in the price change coming from the increase/decrease in the term over which each of the bond's cash flows is discounted

	-The shape of the yield curve - in upward-sloping yield curve environments, for example, the bond will earn positive return as each of the security's cash flows is discounted by a smaller factor.  

Active rolldown return is essentially a function of the portfolio's cash flow distribution along the yield curve relative to its benchmark.  A portfolio that is short duration relative to its benchmark will generally have negative active rolldown return, as long as the yield curve is upward sloping.

ColumnDefinitions.title: Alpha t-stat (Simple)
ColumnDefinitions.columnDesc: The Simple Regression applies a least-squares linear regression calculation to the sub-period portfolio and benchmark returns for the Statistic Period to arrive at a slope that represents the Beta of the portfolio relative to the benchmark and a verticle intercept that represents the Alpha: The portion of the active return that is not explained by the portfolio's beta relative to the benchmark.  The respective t-scores are calculated using the standard 'Student's t-distribution' and reflects the significance or reliability of the regression to describe the active return, with larger t-scores representing a stronger relationship.  As a general rule, a t-stat value greater than or equal to 2 or less than or equal to -2 indicates that the tested metric is significant at 95% confidence.
